posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Rallison makes the following comment regarding regular DCG:

"The glass may be soda lime plate or float glass or most any other kind but it has to be thick enough to withstand the shrinking forces generated during exposure. This means it should be double strength or thicker (3 to 6 mm) for 8 X 10 shots, single strength (2 to 3 mm) for 4 X 5 and 5 X 7, and may be picture glass or as thin as 1 mm for 2 X 2 exposures."

On a side note, the "picture glass" mentioned above (1 mm) is thin glass previously used to cover framed pictures. This is not readily available anymore, and tends to be expensive. It has been replaced by slightly thicker glass which doesn't break as easily as the older, thinner stuff.

On a purely intuitive level, I doubt that plate bowing is your problem with MBDCG, but on the other hand, I always use double strength (3mm) even on 2.5 X 2.5 inch plates (for regular DCG). I also used 3mm glass with 4 X 5 plates with MBDCG without apparent bowing problems (5 minute exposures). There have been quite a few postings of highly successful MBDCG holograms on this forum, without apparent bowing, and I would tend to think they were done on ordinary double-strength glass (3mm or 1/8 inch thick).

posts.author: Sergio
posts.content_md:
Tracing a parallel with a polymer coated onto glass plate, principally after development, not recording, a separated gelatine layer would shrink uniformly in all directions, but on glass plates the the adhesion of polymer on the surface provide a force that opposes any changes in the polymer's shape in the direction parallel to the glass.

The force places the polymer under tensile stress parallel to the plate. The force acts only on the interfacial plane and remains constant while the increasing polymer thickness require a remarkable force increase to maintain the polymer shape.

At some critical force, provided from gelatine development, the emulsion may delaminate, curve the plate or result in nonuniform shrinkage were the middle section of the polymer contracts while the edges remain fixed by the substrate, seems this is your case that may occur with glass thickness of d > 1mm,.

Perhaps a very hard gelatin or different bloom strength can provide a insight to models that can be adapted for a better results.

> Unlike with normal DCG, in MBDCG hardening of the light-struck fringes occurs during exposure.Would you care to elaborate on the rationale behind this statement?

Ok, perhaps I am not entirely knowledgable enough about classic DCG. But the way I understand it, when light strikes a classic DCG emulsion, Cr(6) is converted to Cr(5). The Cr(5) does not crosslink the gelatin. It simply adheres to the nearest gelatin molecule. The actual cross-linking takes place during a dark reaction, or in development in a strong reducing agent such as Sodium metabisulfate, where Cr(5) is donated two electrons and converted to Cr(3).

In MBDCG this is different. A dark reaction is not noticable, and development in SM does not give any benefit (I tried this). So, a logical conclusion is that the cross-linking takes place during exposure. I believe to understand from Jeff's paper that in MBDCG, light strikes the MB, which then goes to a higher energy state. The MB in the highe energy state is able to accept an electron from the electron donor (TMG). When the MB has the extra electron, it is colorless and wants to give it away to someting. That something is the Cr(6) molecule, and upon the next excitation the Cr(5) molecule. When the MB has given away it's electron, it becomes blue again and is ready again for action. (It was discussed in previous subjects that alkaline chromates, thus also MBDCG, do not dark-react.)

Remember that the Leuco (colorless MB) is the actual reducing agent that does all the reducing work in MBDCG. There is no interaction between photons and Cr(6) in MBDCG. It is all done by the MB that has changed into a reducing agent:

> You mean to say that in MBDCG after exposure there is no lueco MB left because of oxygen, yes?

No. I'm just of the opinion that the dark reaction of MBDCG hasn't been adequately investigated. In conventional DCG, the diffraction efficiency continues to be enhanced (by the dark reaction) after very long time periods, even for a month or more after the exposure is stopped. When you say that the dark reaction plays "no role," I think that is a hasty conclusion. It seems to me that if the leuco MB returns to its colored form in several hours, then maybe "several hours" is not long enough to adequately test the usefulness of the dark reaction. If you check the Kubota paper on MBDCG you will find the following comment:

"One method of increasing the sensitivity is to develop the exposed plate after a lapse of time....As is shown in Fig. 1, the required exposure for maximum diffraction efficiency is less for the hologram developed with a time lapse after exposure than for the one developed immediately. This means that the sensitivity of the plate can be increased by having an interval between exposure and development. The exposed plate is stored in a light tight box until development at room temperature (20 - 23C). The sensitivity becomes highest when the plate is developed several days after exposure, and then it reduces with time."

So even without taking any special measures to preserve the leuco state of the MB, he was able to use the dark reaction to considerable advantage with MBDCG. So I'm wondering if the leuco state in preserved as well, perhaps the performance would be even better.

That's why I wanted to try storing the plates under an inert atmosphere, say overnight or longer, so that the leuco MB would stay there longer. As I mentioned before, I can't imagine that the reduction of Cr6 to Cr3 is "instant." In my opinion, I would draw a close parallel between exposed conventional DCG and exposed (leuco) MBDCG.

I'm not "contradicing everything you write" Hans. The essence of my disagreement with you is that I think the dark reaction has promise with MBDCG, and also that I think the reduction of Cr6 to Cr3 is not "instant" as you seem to imply.

> If you check the Kubota paper on MBDCG you will find the following comment:...

Ah, I see now that we are talking about two different things. I have the Kubota/Ose article. They were using a mix of Ammonium Dichromate and MB. But without any electron donor. The recipe from Jeff Blyth uses TMG as an electron donor and it uses Potassium Chromate.

An important difference between Potassium Chromate and Ammonium Dichromate is that Ammonium Dichromate DOES have a dark reaction. MBDCG, mixed with TMG and Potassium Dichromate (or Potassium Chromate) does not dark react. I have coated plates with re-heated six month old MBDCG mixtures and saw no change in behaviour. And I never even stored my MBDCG mixtures in a refrigerator.

So, perhaps the dark reaction that the Kubota paper talks about could be of a different kind than the one you mean:

- It could just be an over-all hardening of the gelatin due to the normal and always present dark-reaction of AmDi in their mix. This increases the available preswell temperature and thus gives the user of the plate the impression of it being more sensitive.

- Or (perhaps not likely/possible), due to the fact that there is no TMG present as an electron donor the MB takes a very long time to get the electron it needs from the surrounding gelatin before it can change into it's Leuco state and reduce the Ammonium Dichromate very quickly indeed.

I think it would be a big step forward for TMG/MBDCG if an "exposed area" dark reaction (if any) could be used to advantage like it is with regular DCG. In regular DCG, both exposed and unexposed areas dark-react, but the exposed areas dark-react more quickly, thus providing a benefit in differential hardening. I've seen how this can be used to considerable advantage in regular DCG, I had hoped the same thing might be possible with MBDCG.

It may be worthwhile to re-open the idea of non-TMG MBDCG, if one is willing to put up with long dark-reaction periods.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
From Jeff's papers on his TMG-DCG system I learnt to pay particular attention to one key feature: there are no dichromates involved here (so far the acronym “DCG” is misleading). There only is chromate, which is far less reactive. So no wonder the dark reaction becomes slow (not to mention the low quantity of potassium chromate present in this system). I guess even in the case where we mixed a coating solution of potassium dichromate, TMG and MB, we would end up having potassium chromate only. The highly alkaline TMG turns the dichromate into chromate. 

Somewhere Rallison mentioned that adding a small amount of TMG to regular DCG improved the shelf life of the DCG layers also. Maybe this is simply due to the presence of chromate.

Thanks Martin, I guess you put your finger on the core of the problem. Now that you mention it, this is what Jianhua Zhu was telling me also, especially about the low chromate concentration.

This all makes me wonder. The reason I'm harping on the dark reaction is because it's really the best way to increase diffraction efficiency. I mean, if you're just letting a plate set it the dark, that's something entirely different from exposing it with laser light, where a host of problems can ruin the hologram, especially for the long exposures. The problem is that people (including myself) tend to be impatient, and want to see results right away. If we got into the habit of delaying processing for a day or longer, we might be able to realize some considerable benefits (assuming we're using a MBDCG system that really does have a light-induced dark reaction that's faster in the exposed areas).

So, even though Jeff's system is very good for processing MBDCG right away, maybe a different MBDCG system would also do well, if a long dark reaction (as suggested by Kubota/Ose) becomes an integral part of the process.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Ok, I now begin to realize that I might have been wrong about plate bending because after more tests the same problem started showing with thicker plates.

I have made one very big mistake with my experiments: I changed more than one thing at a time!!! I started working with a new laser AND at the same time I started using a different setup for exposing. 

- Before I always used a diode laser with great success. Now I use a 20mW HeNe (JDSU 1145/AP). 

- Before I always glued the object to a wooden plank and glued a simple plate holder to the same plank. Now I hold the object and plate in two separate magnetic posts.

When the holograms came out bad, I made two possibly false assumptions:

- I assumed that the new setup was as stable as my old one.

- I assumed that the HeNe laser was more stable than my trusty TEC controlled laser diode.

So, last night I made a Michelson test where I used the plate and object holders as mirror holders. For the leg distances I used the same distance as the maximum I would have had in the Denisyuk MBDCG. The fringes, though very stable and not wobbling at all, moved ever so slowly at the speed of about one fringe per seven minutes. Then I changed the mirror distance, with no effect on the speed of the fringe movements or stability. This makes me suspect that the HeNe is slowly drifting in wavelength. Possibly a gas laser without etalon is not suitable for such long exposures? I phoned JDSU and asked about my model. They stated that these higher power lasers do slowly drift some times due to slow temperature fluctuations of the tube causing changes in mirror spacing. They told me that their lower power lasers are much more suitable for long exposures because less modes are present in the tube at one time. With the Michelson I measured the coherence length of the laser to be about 20cm. That was the distance at which almost no fringes were visible any more. At path differences greater than that, the fringes would come back.

I am very ashamed at drawing such a quick conclusion about glass thickness because I broke a simple law of science: Never assume anything when you change more than one thing at the same time!!! If you have two variables, you need two equations to solve them.

So, now it's time to go back and use the old setup and try that one with the HeNe. If that one gives a good hologram, I will try the new setup and try it with the laser diode. That should solve things nicely.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I just fired up the HeNe again, without touching any of the Michelson parts. While the laser was warming up I could see what it looks like on the interferometer. It looks just like a mode hop in a laser diode. So, that possibly rules out that the problem was with the HeNe, because the fringe drift I saw yesterday was constant and absolutely not jumpy. Whereas changes in laser wavelength appear jumpy on the Michelson: One second the fringes are in one place, the next they are in a another place. The fringes stopped jumping after about 30 minutes, which is more or less conform the specified warmup time of this laser (20 minutes).

Another thing I discovered with this short length Michelson is that my table seems to have an insanely long settling time. The Michelson has been sitting over night and now the fringes are truly rock-solid. Not even a fraction of a fringe movement in a time span of 30 minutes. But it took a night to reach this stability. Need to find out if it is the components that are responsible or that the steel table top is sagging.

So, it's time to go back to the old setup and see if a MBDCG is possible now.
